sections.html:
Norfolk County's largest city, Quincy, sits on Boston Harbor just south of the Neponset River. Boston lies to the north, Milton to the west, Randolph and Braintree to the south, and Weymouth and Hull across the water to the east. In 2020 the census found 101,636 residents, 46,789 households and 51,156 housing units.

The city covers 26.9 square miles, and about 37.6 percent of that is water. A big piece of the land is off the housing market entirely: the Blue Hills Reservation, a state park, takes up roughly 23 percent of the land area in the southwest corner and holds the city's high point, 517-foot Chickatawbut Hill. A house here is either on the harbor side, where Quincy Bay and Wollaston Beach shape daily life, or inland on the hills around Quincy Center, South Quincy and West Quincy.

Buyers search by neighborhood in Quincy, so name yours in any description.

  • Wollaston: an early rail commuter area for Boston workers, now dense and mixed residential and commercial.
  • North Quincy: runs along Hancock Street and Quincy Shore Drive.
  • Quincy Center: the historic commercial and government core, with City Hall and the Thomas Crane Public Library.
  • Quincy Point: densely settled, east of the center, and the site of the Fore River Shipyard.
  • Houghs Neck and Squantum: peninsulas that began as summer resort areas and are now year-round neighborhoods.
  • Marina Bay: built in the 1980s on the former Naval Air Station Squantum, with high-rise condominiums and a large marina.
  • West Quincy: close to Interstate 93, with the old granite quarries.
  • Merrymount, Montclair, Adams Shore, Germantown and South Quincy: mostly residential.

A condo at Marina Bay and a single-family house on Houghs Neck draw different buyers, so pricing and marketing can differ a lot inside one city. The MBTA Red Line has four Quincy stops: North Quincy, Wollaston, Quincy Center and Quincy Adams. Interstate 93 and U.S. 1 run together through the west side, and Routes 3A, 28 and 53 cross the city.

Quincy grew in stages. Granite quarrying dominated 19th century jobs, and the Old Colony Railroad opened in 1845. The population grew by more than 50 percent in the 1920s, and shipbuilding at the Fore River Shipyard carried the 20th century. A single street can hold houses from several eras, and wiring, heating, roofs and smoke alarms can differ sharply from one to the next.

The winters are full New England ones. Average snowfall is 69.7 inches a year across about 29 snowy days, and January lows average 18.3 degrees Fahrenheit. Precipitation totals 53.86 inches a year over about 140 days. Buyers and inspectors look first at roofs, gutters, basements and heating systems, and at anything near Quincy Bay. If your house is close to the shore, ask your insurance agent and the city building department about flood mapping before you list.

State rules govern every sale in Quincy, and the deed goes on record in Norfolk County.

  • Smoke and CO certificate: Your alarms must pass a fire department check before the sale. Reach the Quincy fire department as soon as the closing is scheduled, and budget for the inspection fee.
  • Alarm age: Battery-powered smoke alarms over ten years old, or with no date stamp, get replaced with sealed ten-year photoelectric units that have a hush feature.
  • Deed excise tax: The Norfolk registry charges $2.28 for each $500 of the price on the deed.

Details are on the Mass.gov alarm inspection page and the Norfolk Registry fee schedule. The statute behind the rate is G.L. c. 64D, section 1.

Real estate tax in Quincy comes in four quarterly bills. Bills one and two are preliminary, together about 50 percent of last year's tax, due August 1 and November 1. Bills three and four apply the new assessed value and the current rate, less what you already paid, and fall due February 1 and May 1.

Property record cards are posted online, and a new valuation appears on the third-quarter bill each January. The assessors are at 1305 Hancock Street, phone (617) 376-1170. See the Quincy Assessors page for bill explanations.

An overvalued house can be challenged by filing an abatement application. It must reach the assessors by the date the first installment is due, which in a quarterly city is generally February 1. Three months is how long the assessors have to answer. After their decision, three more months remain to take the case to the Appellate Tax Board. Late payments put the appeal at risk, so stay current while it moves.

If a sale is coming up this year, ask your closing attorney how the current quarter will be split at the table. Gather recent sales of comparable nearby houses and photographs before you file, since the owner carries the burden of showing the value is too high. A short, specific case does better than a general complaint, and the property record card posted online is a good place to check the facts the city holds on your house.

Most delays come from documents, not from the house. Before you speak with a buyer or an attorney, put these in one place: your deed, the latest tax bill, any permit records, a list of repairs you know the house needs and the contact details for the Quincy fire department.

If a mortgage is still open, ask your lender for a payoff figure. If you are selling an inherited house, talk to a probate attorney about court authority first. Then compare the routes side by side: a standard listing with repairs and showings, or a cash offer with a closing date you pick. Cash Home Buyers can buy a Quincy house in its present condition, and you can say no to any offer. Either way, the recording step at the Norfolk registry stays the same.

Sellers in Quincy tend to land in one of four situations, each with a sensible first move.

  • A house that needs work: get a rough repair list before choosing between listing and a cash sale, so you compare real net numbers.
  • Alarm and certificate timing: book the fire department early so a missed inspection does not delay closing.
  • An inherited house: the estate may need court authority before it can sell, so talk to a probate attorney first.
  • Tight timelines: a job move or a payment problem favors a quick, certain closing over a long marketing period.

Every route, from a standard listing to a cash offer, ends at the same Norfolk County recording step. What differs is how many repairs, showings and weeks you need before you get there.

faqs.a: Quincy covers 26.9 square miles, about 37.6 percent of it water, and had 101,636 residents at the 2020 census.
Yes. Quincy deeds are recorded at the Norfolk Registry of Deeds.

faqs.q: Do I need a smoke and carbon monoxide certificate to sell in Quincy?
faqs.a: Yes. The fire department has to certify that the alarms meet state standards before a sale or transfer, so book the visit once a closing date is set.

faqs.q: What is the deed excise rate in Quincy?
faqs.a: The Norfolk registry collects $2.28 for each $500 of the price stated on the deed. Your attorney will work out the exact amount for your sale.

faqs.q: When are Quincy property taxes due?
faqs.a: Four times a year: August 1, November 1, February 1 and May 1.
